title: German Luxury Car Maker
concepts_tested: unit cost build-up (manufacturing, transport, customs, SG&A)
prompt: Our client is a German luxury car maker. They have come to us as they want to grow their business and are looking into selling their cars in Bangladesh. The GDP growth in Bangladesh is 5% per year. Currently, the only luxury car sold in Bangladesh is Mercedes-Benz, and they have been in the market for the past 10 years. The CEO wants to find out if the company enters the market, can they break even in three years?

clarifying_info.answer: Mercedes-Benz imported and sold 10,000 cars in this market over the past 10 years, and has their own dealership in Bangladesh.
There are 1,000 new luxury vehicle buyers each year.
The average selling price of a luxury vehicle in Bangladesh is $100,000.
Existing owners replace their car every 10 years.

The client will have a 30% market share each year (not given out right away — candidate should be asked to brainstorm how to estimate market share first; a benchmark is available: the client already entered Vietnam and other markets similar to Bangladesh and gained 30% market share on average in each).

interviewer_notes: Candidate-led case (interviewee led) testing market entry with a market-sizing build (replacement demand + new buyers), a detailed unit cost build-up, and a breakeven calculation, followed by a competitive-response risk brainstorm. Ratings: Quant - 2, Qual - 2, Overall - 2 (book's own scale).

suggested_framework.summary: Book-provided framework covering market, product, customers, financial analysis, and risks of entering the Bangladesh luxury car market.

tree.label: German luxury car maker entering Bangladesh

children.label: How are cars similar or different?
Do we have the same branding?
Fixed Costs: Overhead, SG&A, Set-up costs

stages.interviewer_asks: How would you think about whether the company should enter the Bangladesh luxury car market and whether it can break even in three years?
stages.expected_answer: A framework covering market (industry size/growth/trends, competition), product (similarity to competitor, branding), customers (brand loyalty, interest, willingness-to-pay drivers), financial analysis (revenue: price and volume; cost: variable and fixed), and risks (geopolitical: tariffs, political instability; competition: price war, new entrants).
good_answer_signals: Structures around market, product, customers, financials, and risk
Recognizes breakeven analysis will require both a market-sizing step and a unit-economics step

stages.interviewer_asks: How would you estimate the total addressable market size and our client's likely market share?
stages.info_to_release: Mercedes-Benz sold 10,000 cars in Bangladesh over the past 10 years and has its own dealership. There are 1,000 new luxury vehicle buyers each year. The average selling price of a luxury vehicle in Bangladesh is $100,000. Existing owners replace their car every 10 years. Market share information (30%, based on the client's past entries into Vietnam and similar markets) should not be given out right away — ask the candidate to first brainstorm how to estimate market share (e.g., via customer needs survey, or by finding a comparable benchmark).
stages.release_when: Give market share (30%) only after the candidate has proposed an approach to estimating it.
stages.expected_answer: Existing owner base = 10,000 cars sold over 10 years; with a 10-year replacement cycle, 10,000/10 = 1,000 replacement cars are sold per year. Adding 1,000 new luxury vehicle buyers per year gives a total annual market size of 2,000 cars per year. Total market revenue = 2,000 cars × $100,000/car = $200,000,000. With a 30% market share (benchmarked from the client's past entries into Vietnam and similar markets), the client would sell 2,000 × 30% = 600 cars per year.
good_answer_signals: Recognizes the 10,000-car installed base implies 1,000 replacement sales per year via the 10-year replacement cycle
Adds replacement demand and new-buyer demand together rather than using only one
Proposes a reasonable method for estimating market share before being given the 30% benchmark (e.g., survey-based fit assessment or comparable-market benchmarking)

stages.interviewer_asks: Given the cost structure, what is the profit per car, and can the client break even in three years?
stages.info_to_release: Initial investment: $7M. Cost per car: Manufacturing $20K; Transportation = 120% of Manufacturing cost; Customs/Taxes = 95% of (Manufacturing + Transportation); SG&A = 12% of all the above costs. Selling price: $100,000/car. Market share: 30%. Total market: 2,000 cars/year.
stages.expected_answer: Transportation = 120% × $20K = $24K. Customs/Taxes = 95% × ($20K + $24K) = 95% × $44K = $41.8K. SG&A = 12% × ($20K + $24K + $41.8K) = 12% × $85.8K ≈ $10.3K. Total variable cost per car ≈ $20K + $24K + $41.8K + $10.3K = $96.1K, rounding to $96K/car. Profit per car = $100K - $96K = $4K. Annual profit at 30% market share = 2,000 cars × 30% × $4K/car = 600 cars × $4K = $2.4M/year. Breakeven period = $7M initial investment / $2.4M annual profit ≈ 2.9 years, i.e., roughly 3 years — the client can break even in 3 years.
good_answer_signals: Builds each cost component sequentially in the correct order (transportation off manufacturing, customs off the sum of both, SG&A off the sum of all three)
Correctly computes profit per car and then annual profit using market share and total market volume
Divides the $7M initial investment by annual profit to get the breakeven period and connects it back to the CEO's 3-year target

stages.interviewer_asks: Evaluate potential risks of entering this market.
stages.expected_answer: Assumptions used in the analysis might be inaccurate. Bangladesh is not stable politically and economically, so the client will bear more risk. There could be other new entrants. Mercedes-Benz could react to the entry by reducing price (though with the low income level in the country, customers who can afford luxury cars might not be very price sensitive) — a candidate should note Mercedes-Benz could cut price to $96K/car or below (the client's cost) to make the client's entry unprofitable — or by improving their service if that's the client's differentiating factor.
good_answer_signals: Identifies assumption risk, macro/political risk, new-entrant risk, and specifically Mercedes-Benz's likely competitive response
When asked how low Mercedes-Benz could cut price, correctly reasons it could go to the client's cost level ($96K/car) or below
Notes that low-income-country luxury buyers may be less price-sensitive, tempering the price-war risk

stages.interviewer_asks: What is your recommendation to the CEO?
stages.expected_answer: The profit on each car is $4K. With a 30% market share, the client's annual profit will be $2.4M, and the client will break even in 3 years, so the CEO's target is achievable. Risks include those raised in the brainstorming (assumption risk, political/economic instability, new entrants, Mercedes-Benz's competitive response). Next steps: market analysis on competitive response and target customer; determine the best way to enter the market (JV, greenfield, etc.); look into ownership structure (franchise or owned showrooms).
good_answer_signals: Directly answers the CEO's original question (breakeven in 3 years) with the supporting numbers
Proposes a price-sensitivity analysis to determine the correct price, and proactively raises how to estimate market share as ways to strengthen the analysis
Names concrete next steps on entry mode and ownership structure

math.question: What is the total annual luxury car market size in Bangladesh?
givens: Mercedes-Benz sold 10,000 cars over the past 10 years
Existing owners replace their car every 10 years
1,000 new luxury vehicle buyers each year
steps: Replacement demand per year = 10,000 cars / 10 years = 1,000 cars/year
New buyer demand per year = 1,000 cars/year
math.answer: 2,000 cars/year total market size ($200M in annual revenue)

math.question: What is the profit per car, the client's annual profit at 30% market share, and how many years to break even on the $7M initial investment?
givens: SG&A: 12% of all the above costs
steps: Breakeven period = $7M / $2.4M ≈ 2.9 years, rounds to ~3 years
math.answer: Profit per car ≈ $4K; annual profit ≈ $2.4M; breakeven in ≈3 years

synthesis: The profit on each car is $4K. With a 30% market share, the client's annual profit will be $2.4M, and the client will break even in 3 years — the CEO's target is achievable, though risks from brainstorming (political/economic instability, competitive response, new entrants) should be further investigated.
what_great_looks_like: Recognizes the installed base implies a recurring replacement-demand stream, not just new-buyer demand, when sizing the market
Proposes a sound method for estimating market share (survey-based fit, or comparable-market benchmark) before being handed the 30% figure
Builds the per-car cost stack in the correct sequential order (transportation on manufacturing, customs on the sum, SG&A on the total)
Connects the $2.4M annual profit and $7M investment directly to the CEO's original 3-year breakeven question
Reasons precisely about how low Mercedes-Benz could cut price in response ($96K, the client's own cost) rather than giving a vague 'they might lower prices' answer
common_pitfalls: Sizing the market using only new buyers (1,000/year) and ignoring the replacement-cycle demand from the existing 10,000-car base
Applying each cost percentage to the wrong base (e.g., applying SG&A to only manufacturing cost instead of the sum of all prior costs)
Giving the market share (30%) without first asking the candidate to reason about how to estimate it
Treating the breakeven answer as a simple yes/no without surfacing the risks that could undermine the estimate
